newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ brokerage cuts back, says industry to be hit.
newsitem.headline: NZ brokerage cuts back, says industry to be hit.

text.p: An independent New Zealand brokerage said on Thursday it was slashing staff to 16 from 27 and suggested a big shake-up in the industry loomed.
Garlick & Co Managing Director and 71 percent owner, Bill Garlick, said his firm had undergone its fourth restructuring in 11 years.
"We have realigned the business to meet what we see as the evolving trends," Garlick told Reuters.
"The New Zealand broking industry is going to have the most extraordinary shake-out in the next two years."
"We thought we saw a shake-out after the crash of '87. The sort of shakeout we are going to see in New Zealand broking will rival that."

Reasons he cited were the popularity of investing in passive unmanaged funds, a squeeze on margins, regionalisation of funds management activities and competition to sell securities from non-industry markets, particularly the internet.
Stock Exchange chairman David Wale saw no major shake-up for the industry but at the same time did not deny "futuristic" issues such as internet trading had to be faced.
"Nobody else has laid off anybody," Wale told Reuters.
He described the market as quiet, blaming the hangover from last year's election uncertainty and concern about Wall Street.
"This year the market has declined six to seven percent but if you looked at volumes they are not that dire."
Garlick said his firm was outsourcing more work to international firms with which it already had alliances.

"The market is changing so quickly -- if you are going to remain in our position as a viable operator, you have to keep shifting your business and anticipate where the markets are going," Garlick said.
He had looked at selling to an international firm but rejected that option.

Recent low and declining turnover on the Stock Exchange was not cyclical, he said. But the introduction of a warrant market recently would help alleviate declining turnover in the underlying market by providing additional liquidity.
Foreign ownership of a greater proportion of corporates was also affecting turnover, he said.
And there had been few floats of any significance in the last 12 months.
The recent move of the New Zealand operations of life office Prudential to Sydney was likely to be part of a growing trend of Australasian and Asia-wide regionalism, he said.
"The trends are very clear indeed," Garlick said.
He denied that failure to clean up shady dealings in the New Zealand market in the wake of the 1987 stockmarket crash was a factor in declining small investor interest.
In fact, Garlick argued the securities regulatory regime was so restrictive it was helping to strangle the market.
